new_statements.quote: The Ok languages, the central and eastern Mek languages, and the Dani languages west of Angguruk have two series of stops. The Yale language and the Angguruk language have only one series. In Eipomek and in the dialects east of Eipomek, accent is phonemic. Angguruk places the accent on the last syllable, and the Yale language tends to place it on the last syllable.
new_statements.citation: Heeschen, Volker. 1992. The position of the Mek languages of Irian Jaya among the Papuan languages; history, typology, and speech. Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde 148(3/4): 465-488. doi:10.1163/22134379-90003146
new_statements.locator: p. 470 (section on Mek-Dani contacts; PDF page 7)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (+.txt text layer, lines 255-264 = journal p.470). The quoted passage is there word for word: 'The Ok languages, the central and eastern Mek languages, and the Dani languages west of Angguruk have two series of stops. The Yale language and the Angguruk language have only one series. In Eipomek and in the dialects east of Eipomek, accent is phonemic. Angguruk places the accent on the last syllable, and the Yale language tends to place it on the last syllable.' No other stress/accent/tone remark in the article (grepped accent|stress|tone|tonal|syllable). Identity: p.466 of the same article lists the Mek groups and defines '1. in the north-west, the Yale language spoken around Kosarek,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent in Yale is not phonemic (contrast drawn with Eipomek and eastern Mek, where it is); it tends to fall on the final syllable of the word, an areal trait shared with neighbouring Angguruk Yali. Stated as a tendency, not an exceptionless rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None specified; the hedge 'tends to' implies exceptions exist but they are not described here. Heeschen 1978:12-13 separately reports (second-hand, Bromley 1973:15) that 'tones are said to be phonemic in Nalca and Kosarek', adding that he found no minimal pairs and that tonal features arise only in restricted environments (syllable contraction, final glottal stop).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent, stated in a brief areal-typological comparison by the language's principal fieldworker; no discussion of phrase vs citation forms. The full first-hand phonology (Heeschen 1992 dictionary, pp. 9-14; Heeschen 2000/2010 sketch) was not accessible and may refine or qualify this.
new_statements.identity_note: Heeschen's 'Yale language' = the language of the Yalenang of the Kosarek area (In/Denkomne valleys), i.e. Glottolog kosa1249 Kosarek Yale / ISO kkl; not to be confused with Yali (Dani family, e.g. Angguruk Yali) or Yale/Yade of PNG (yale1246). The statement is a one-sentence areal remark in a comparative article, not a dialect-specific phonology.

sources.note: pp.12-13 (section 1.2 Diversity of the Mek languages): 'Stress seems to be partially phonemic in the east, e.g. Ok Bab 'uku "fire" and u'ku..., while tones are said to be phonemic in Nalca and Kosarek (Bromley 1973:15 and Rule and Cutting). Though I have not found any minimal pair in Nalca and Kosarek, the development of (non) phonemic tones can be explained by two processes...' i.e. second-hand tone claim for Kosarek, doubted by Heeschen; section 2.1 (p.23) gives explicit stress rules but for Eipo only, not Yale. Image-only scan, scanned with tesseract, key sentences verified on page images.
